content: To reduce selenium exposure in drinking water, alternative water sources can be used, or low-selenium water sources can be blended with high-selenium ones. Selenium removal methods may also be considered. A case of selenium toxicity was reported from well water containing 9 mg/L of selenium. Dietary selenium intake associated with selenosis exceeds 900 µg/day. Selenium is an essential element, and recommended daily intakes have been established by various organizations. For infants and children, the recommended intake ranges from 6–21 µg/day, depending on age. For adolescent females and males, the recommended intakes are 26 µg/day and 30 µg/day, respectively. For adult females and males, the recommended intakes are 26 µg/day and 35 µg/day, respectively. Due to concerns about adverse effects from excessive selenium exposure, upper limits have been set, with the FAO/WHO establishing a tolerable upper limit of 400 µg/day. Silver occurs naturally, primarily as insoluble sulfides, oxides, and salts. In drinking water, silver is most commonly found as ionic compounds like silver nitrate (soluble) and silver chloride (relatively insoluble). Silver can also exist as nanoparticles, which may enter water bodies through wastewater or industrial discharges. When silver is used in point-of-use water treatment devices, drinking water becomes the primary source of silver exposure. Silver concentrations in surface and groundwater are typically below 5 µg/L, though rare detections above 100 µg/L have been reported. A formal tolerable daily intake (TDI) for silver could not be derived due to data limitations. However, 6 mg/kg body weight/day of colloidal silver was considered a lowest observed adverse effect level (LOAEL) based on a case of argyria in a woman who ingested this dose for 16 months. Argyria, characterized by skin and hair discoloration due to silver deposition in tissues, is the only clear sign of silver overload. The toxicological database for silver is insufficient to establish a formal guideline value, but a provisional reference value of 1 mg/L in drinking water has been suggested as a benchmark. Simazine, a pre-emergence herbicide, is persistent and mobile in the environment. It is not genotoxic in mammalian systems. Recent studies have shown an increase in mammary tumors in female rats but no effects in mice. The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) has classified simazine as Group 3, meaning it is not classifiable as to its carcinogenicity to humans. Sodium dichloroisocyanurate, a sodium salt of chlorinated hydroxytriazine, is used as a source of free chlorine for water disinfection. It is widely used for disinfecting swimming pools, in the food industry, and for emergency drinking water disinfection. The guideline values for sodium dichloroisocyanurate and its byproduct cyanuric acid are 50 mg/L and 40 mg/L, respectively. Sodium dichloroisocyanurate has low acute oral toxicity and does not induce genotoxic, carcinogenic, or teratogenic effects. The no-observed-effect level (NOEL) for sodium cyanurate was based on urinary tract and cardiac lesions observed in male rats at higher doses. Styrene, primarily used in plastics and resins, is found in trace amounts in water, food, and air. In industrial areas, air exposure can lead to daily intakes of a few hundred micrograms, with smoking increasing exposure up to tenfold. Styrene is rapidly absorbed and distributed in the body, preferentially in lipid-rich tissues, and is metabolized to styrene-7,8-oxide, a direct-acting mutagen. Metabolites are excreted in urine. Styrene has low acute toxicity but has shown mutagenic effects in vitro with metabolic activation. Chromosomal aberrations have been observed in vitro and in vivo, mostly at high doses. Long-term studies showed increased lung tumors in mice at high doses but no carcinogenic effects in rats. Styrene-7,8-oxide was carcinogenic in rats. IARC classifies styrene as Group 2B, possibly carcinogenic to humans. Sulfates occur naturally in many minerals and are used in the chemical industry. They are discharged into water through industrial waste and atmospheric deposition, with the highest levels typically found in groundwater from natural sources. The average daily intake of sulfate is approximately 500 mg, primarily from food. In areas with high sulfate levels in drinking water, water may become the principal source of intake. Existing data do not identify a level of sulfate in drinking water likely to cause adverse health effects. Studies indicate a laxative effect at concentrations of 1000–1200 mg/L but no increase in diarrhea, dehydration, or weight loss. No health-based guideline is proposed for sulfate, but authorities should be notified if drinking water sources exceed 500 mg/L. Sulfate may also affect water taste and contribute to the corrosion of distribution systems.
